title: "Predicting Urban Pulse"
subtitle: "An End-to-End Econometric and Machine Learning Framework for Traffic Forecasting"
author: "Tyler Stigall"
date: "2026-07-07"
abstract: |
  This technical report details the development, backtesting, and out-of-sample deployment of competing predictive architectures to forecast daily cyclist volumes on Victoria's Johnson Street Bridge infrastructure. By evaluating a baseline OLS model against a classical econometric ARIMAX framework and a Gradient Boosted Trees architecture (XGBoost), this paper analyzes model resilience during seasonal demand regime shifts.
---

## Executive Context & Objectives

The **Johnson Street Bridge** serves as a critical active transportation artery in the Capital Regional District (CRD). For municipal planners and transit engineers, understanding ridership patterns is essential for optimizing winter maintenance windows, scheduling structural repairs, and justifying long-term infrastructure funding.

The core objective of this project is to construct a reproducible data pipeline capable of digesting urban counter data and outputting high-precision, short-to-medium-term demand projections.

::: {.callout-note}
## Project Stack
This entire analysis is fully reproducible and compiled using **R, XGBoost, the forecast library, and Quarto**. The structural logic is isolated across five atomic scripts within the repository ecosystem.
:::

## Integrated Data Strategy

Our predictive pipeline synthesizes multiple distinct data channels:

1. **Ridership Baseline:** Automated daily cyclist counts extracted directly from the public Eco-Counter platform tracking the Johnson Street Multi-Use Pathway (MUD).
2. **Meteorological Regressors:** Historical and realized weather arrays (including mean daily temperature, precipitation volume, and average wind speeds) integrated via the `openmeteo` API.
3. **Feature Engineering:** Indicator variables mapping calendar anomalies, day-of-week demand patterns, and multi-week auto-regressive momentum components.

## Analytical Methodology

To robustly evaluate predictive capacity, we implement a multi-model bake-off framework:

* **Ordinary Least Squares (OLS):** Established strictly as an environmental baseline to isolate the flat, linear impact of weather variations without temporal memory.
* **ARIMAX(14, 1, 1)(1, 0, 0):** A classical econometric time-series framework engineered to track structural weekly momentum and autoregressive errors.
* **XGBoost:** A non-linear machine learning architecture designed to capture complex feature interactions, such as sudden weather-driven "demand cliffs."

## Out-of-Sample Production Results

The models were fully trained on historical data and deployed to generate true out-of-sample predictions for the entire month of November 2025. Evaluating these forecasts against realized counts on the bridge yielded a definitive performance hierarchy:

| Model Architecture | MAE (Daily Riders) | RMSE | MAPE (%) | Production Status |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| **XGBoost (Machine Learning)** | **233.18** | **285.63** | **14.99%** | 🏆 **Selected for Deployment** |
| ARIMAX(14, 1, 1)(1, 0, 0) | 287.36 | 370.29 | 20.21% | Deployed Baseline |
| Linear Regression (OLS) | 318.65 | 418.81 | 21.51% | Environmental Benchmark |

: November 2025 Production Performance Metrics
